description_full: Park-Ohio Holdings Corp. provides supply chain management outsourcing services, capital equipment, and manufactured components in the United States, Europe, Asia, Mexico, Canada, and internationally. The company operates through three segments: Supply Technologies, Assembly Components, and Engineered Products. The Supply Technologies segment offers Total Supply Management, a solution that manages aspects of supplying production parts and materials, such as engineering and design support, part usage and cost analysis, supplier selection, quality assurance, bar coding, product packaging and tracking, just-in-time and point-of-use delivery, electronic billing services, and ongoing technical support. This segment also provides production components, including valves, fuel hose assemblies, electro-mechanical hardware, labels, fittings, and steering components; and precision cold-formed and cold-extruded fasteners, and locknuts, as well as nuts, bolts, and wheel hardware under the SPAC brand. The Assembly Components segment offers high pressure direct fuel injection fuel rails and pipes; fuel filler pipes; plastic and rubber assemblies; Turbo Charging and Turbo Coolant hoses; and design engineering, machining, and parts assembly value-added services. The Engineered Products segment provides field services, induction heating and melting systems, pipe threading systems, and forged and machined products for the ferrous and non-ferrous metals, silicon, coatings, forging, foundry, automotive, and construction equipment industries. This segment also engineers and installs mechanical forging presses; sells spare parts, machine, induction harden, and surface finish crankshafts and camshafts for use in locomotives; and forge aerospace and defense structural components comprising landing gears and struts, and railcar center plate and draft lug rail products. Park-Ohio Holdings Corp. was founded in 1907 and is headquartered in Cleveland, Ohio.

financial_summary: Park-Ohio Holdings Corp. is a small-cap industrials business with a $658M market cap on $1.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +1% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 19% against a 10% cost of capital — a 9-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 16% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $2M in free cash flow — roughly 0 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.78× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 1.4× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 1.2%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 31% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.4× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Piotroski score 4/9 — below the median for a healthy business
Altman Z in the grey zone — financial health warrants monitoring
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $2.6M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Industrials sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 6% over 3 months
Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.
